extracted.intended_audience: students of American government and politics (civics/undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate the procedural rules, powers, and practices governing the transaction of legislative business in the U.S. House and Senate, with emphasis on the Speaker, rules committee, standing committees, debate limits, and obstruction tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker may refuse purely dilatory motions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker has regular sanction for refusing to entertain purely dilatory motions (a principle embodied in the rules after 1890).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when ordinary parliamentary motions are being used solely for delay and obstruction; it is the duty of the occupant of the Speaker's chair to take the proper course under parliamentary law. Example: Speaker may refuse to entertain motions aimed only at obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional right to demand yeas and nays cannot be denied
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the purpose is dilatory, the constitutional right of a member to demand the yeas and nays cannot be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Speaker may refuse dilatory motions, a member's demand for recorded roll-call votes (yeas and nays) remains a protected constitutional right and must be respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker may count as present members who refuse to answer roll-call
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker may count as present those members physically present but who refuse to answer to their names on a roll-call for the purpose of compelling an adjournment in the absence of a quorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle established by Speaker Reed and embodied in the rules to prevent quorum-evading tactics; supports continuing business when quorum is physically present despite evasive behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-hour limit on individual debate
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules prescribe that the time occupied by any member in discussing a legislative proposition shall not exceed one hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imposed in 1841; a member may yield a portion of his time to others but may occupy no more than one hour except by unanimous consent. He may not speak twice on the same measure unless he introduced it or is reporting it from committee. When in Committee of the Whole, the House fixes debate time which the committee cannot extend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yielding and speaking limitations on debate
rubrics_metrics.description: A member may yield a portion of his time to other members but cannot exceed the one-hour limit and generally may not speak twice on the same measure except in specified cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: the introducer or committee reporter may speak more than once; unanimous consent can extend time. Committee of the Whole sets fixed debate time that cannot be extended by the committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain committees may report practically at any time
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific committees may report on enumerated subjects practically at any time in the course of House procedure (e.g., rules, elections, ways and means, appropriations, rivers and harbors, public lands, territories, enrolled bills, invalid pensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision enables party leaders to bring measures up when they see fit and is a major instrument by which party control is exercised over the House's agenda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules committee privileged procedural powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The committee on rules may report at any time; its reports are highly privileged and only a motion to adjourn may be entertained during consideration of its report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It can recommend making a bill a 'special order' for a certain day, determine how much time is given to measures, what order they are taken up in, and may propose resolutions to stop debate on particular measures and force adoption or rejection. Its recommendations are subject to House approval and depend on measuring the majority's temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: House committees conduct most legislative work and control outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative work of each house is done largely by committees, and every committee is controlled by a majority of members representing the dominant party; only bills reported favorably from committees have much chance of being acted upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees frequently originate bills (notably appropriations), secure documents and witnesses, hold hearings, and draft measures. A bill reported favorably enjoys high probability of passage; committees can effectively veto measures by delaying or ignoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee options for a referred bill
rubrics_metrics.description: With regard to any measure referred to it, a committee may recommend adoption, amend it, report adversely, delay the report indefinitely, or ignore it altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the House it is rare for a member to secure consideration of a bill the committee opposes; the Senate usually offers greater freedom in this respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcommittees and majority control within committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures in charge of a committee are usually considered or formulated by a subcommittee (in which the minority receives scant recognition), and the whole committee generally accepts the subcommittee's report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On party questions, majority members of the committee draft the bill and may invite minority members to vote as a matter of form; this concentrates power in the committee majority and its subcommittees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committees may obtain executive information and hold hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: On measures of vital importance, committees may secure papers and documents from executive departments, request officers to appear personally, and hold hearings with witnesses similar to courtroom procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearings may be held in various parts of the country; witnesses may be required to attend and give evidence; this provides committees investigatory and fact-finding capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee proliferation and need for coordination
rubrics_metrics.description: Division into many separate committees with narrow jurisdictions can lead to measures being shaped with little reference to other committees, producing ill-adjusted or conflicting legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the committee on ways and means has no official communication with appropriations committees, making revenue-expenditure balancing difficult. Recommendation: recognize chairmen accountability or otherwise secure responsibility in committee leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee assignments determined by party caucuses/leadership ('higgling')
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee assignments are effectively determined by party caucuses and leaders (a process described as 'higgling in the market'), with prestigious assignments falling according to seniority, ability, and management skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically committees were appointed by the Speaker; reforms moved toward election by the House but selection via caucuses remains dominant; minority party selects its committee members similarly but with less influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: House practice: many important measures taken under special orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all important measures before the House are dealt with under special orders from the rules committee, giving that committee practical control of the course of business in the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special-order resolutions can curb debate and define procedures that expedite passage; minority protections (e.g., time for minority members) can be curtailed under such orders as illustrated in record extracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanimous consent and Speaker's ability to block ordinary members
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordinary member can bring his own measures up for discussion only with the 'unanimous consent of the House,' and the Speaker, as a member, may object and thus prevent the matter being brought up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: members often must visit the Speaker in advance to secure his approval; the Speaker historically used this prerogative to control what received consideration and to reward or withhold favors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee of the Whole rules and quorum
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Committee of the Whole, 100 constitute a quorum and the Speaker's chair is taken by another member; measures approved in it are reported to the House for formal adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the House goes into Committee of the Whole it fixes the time of debate which the committee cannot extend; Committee of the Whole is a convenient body for discussion and provisional voting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate permits prolonged debate (filibuster) absent drastic House methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate has not adopted the drastic methods obtaining in the House; obstruction in the Senate is ordinarily by prolonged speaking and any member with sufficient endurance may prevent a measure coming to a vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice can force the majority to capitulate or extract concessions (e.g., insertion of special appropriations). Attempts to restore the previous question were omitted in 1806 and have failed; in 1908 some principles were applied to limit certain obstruction tactics (see related items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate 1908 procedural limits (quorum/recurrence/speech repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles applied in 1908: (1) the presiding officer may refuse to comply with a demand for a roll-call on a quorum if, on a count, he finds a quorum present; (2) the question of 'no quorum' cannot be again raised after the roll has been called and a quorum found present unless other legislative business has intervened; (3) the dormant rule that a Senator may not speak on the same subject more than once on the same day may be revived at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These house rules were intended to defeat tactics of prolonged debate and to limit recurrence of quorum calls used to obstruct business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileged status of certain motions and reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of the rules committee and certain motions (e.g., motions to take a recess when specified) are privileged and take precedence over ordinary motions such as adjournment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example privileged resolution: closing debate by motion before going into Committee of the Whole, not subject to amendment or debate; such privileges expedite business but limit minority procedural options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical control by the Speaker (appointment and recognition powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the Speaker had the power to appoint all committees and name chairmen, to recognize whomsoever he pleased on the floor, to refuse dilatory motions, and to decide parliamentary procedure, thereby exerting near-absolute control over legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Speaker Cannon's regime where speakers exercised private objections to block unanimous-consent requests, required members to seek private approval in the Speaker's chamber, and leveraged committee appointments and rules to control new members.
